title: GEOLOGICAL SURVEY OF VICTORIA. COMPOSITE ATLAS of seventy-one maps.
description: GEOLOGICAL SURVEY OF VICTORIA. COMPOSITE ATLAS of seventy-one maps. Oblong folio, 71 colour lithographed maps, with some additional highlights and text by hand, approximately 450 x 600 mm., many mounted to backing sheets within inked double-line borders, a few loosely inserted (one of these with a stamp on verso), also some sheets left blank: condition is substantially good but with some creasing, staining, marginal splits, flecking (particularly of the mounts), and tape repairs, in modern calf boards (bowed) with marbled endpapers, the Index Map browned and with loss through flecking. Melbourne, Crown Lands Office, 1862ff. The Survey’s first four quarter sheets, the Melbourne metropolitan area, were originally issued in 1860 and are here complete in issues of 1863-1864. “Since no reliable topographic maps existed, Selwyn’s geologists had to create their own, precisely surveying every gully and hill before they could overlay the geological details. Of the four years (1858-62) it took Ulrich and Aplin to complete the Castlemaine quarter sheets, three were spent in mapping the topography. In the course of their Castlemaine mapping, Aplin and Ulrich climbed into 3,000 diggers’ holes and dug 81 of their own.” See https://earthresources.vic.gov.au. The album is apparently an owner’s compilation from the 1860s, with nine maps dated between 1901 and 1942. Two of the original foolscap Geological Reports are laid in (one with torn wrappers). Some of the earlier maps are lithographed by Thomas Ham and by David Tulloch. Estimate $4400/6600 Lot 10

title: BARRINGTON, George. THE HISTORY OF NEW SOUTH WALES, including Botany Bay, Port Jackson, Parramatta, Sydney, and all its
description: BARRINGTON, George. THE HISTORY OF NEW SOUTH WALES, including Botany Bay, Port Jackson, Parramatta, Sydney, and all its dependencies from the original discovery of the island. Octavo, with engraved title with coloured vignette, handcoloured frontispiece and 13 plates, plus an additional four plates, full-page woodcut in-text, bound without the list of plates in recent half calf. London, Printed for M. Jones, 1802. First edition. The first book with handcoloured topographical views of New South Wales. The History was clearly such a success that Jones decided to prepare a ‘prequel’, describing the voyage from England to Botany Bay, for publication in 1803, with a new edition of both volumes in 1810. Perhaps the best known of all ‘Barrington’ pieces, this elaborate production was originally issued in parts over 1802 and subsequently sold bound up in volume form. The book has “no real relationship with the earlier 1795 ‘Barrington’ Voyage apart from the unauthorised use of his [Barrington’s] name… In fact [it is] largely extracted, more or less verbatim, from David Collins’s two-volume account” (Wantrup). title: BIGGE, John Thomas. A COMPLETE SET OF THE THREE REPORTS into the State of the Colony of New South Wales, the Judicial Es
description: BIGGE, John Thomas. A COMPLETE SET OF THE THREE REPORTS into the State of the Colony of New South Wales, the Judicial Establishments of New South Wales and Van Diemen’s Land, and the State of Agriculture and Trade [with] A Copy of the Instructions given by Earl Bathurst to Mr. Bigge, on his proceeding to New South Wales. Bigge was appointed Royal Commissioner by Lord Bathurst to examine the transportation system, but “it was clear that Macquarie’s administration as much as the transportation system was under review… Bigge’s reports had a profound influence on the future constitutional and political development of Australia and have a place in any Australian collection” (Wantrup). title: COLLINS, David. AN ACCOUNT OF THE ENGLISH COLONY IN NEW SOUTH WALES, with Remarks on the Dispositions, Customs, Manners, &c.
description: COLLINS, David. AN ACCOUNT OF THE ENGLISH COLONY IN NEW SOUTH WALES, with Remarks on the Dispositions, Customs, Manners, &c. of the Native Inhabitants of that Country. To which are added, some particulars of New Zealand; compiled, by permission, from the Mss. of Lieutenant-Governor King... [together with] AN ACCOUNT OF THE ENGLISH COLONY IN NEW SOUTH WALES, from its first Settlement, in January 1788, to August 1801: with Remarks on the Dispositions, Customs, Manners, &c. of the Native Inhabitants of that Country. To which are added, some particulars of New Zealand; compiled, by permission, from the Mss. of Lieutenant-Governor King; and an account of a voyage performed by Captain Flinders and Mr Bass; by which the existence of a Strait separating Van Diemen’s Land from the continent of New Holland was ascertained. Abstracted from the Journal of Mr Bass... Vol. II. Two volumes, quarto, containing in total two maps, 23 plates, (three coloured) and eight half-page engravings (two coloured), some foxing and offsetting as usual, uniformly bound with both half-titles in speckled calf of the epoch, early (probably contemporary) typographical bookplate of John Rutherford of Edgerston, London, Printed by A. Strahan for T. Cadell and W. Davies, 1798 – 1802. First and best editions: a handsome set in uniform contemporary bindings. Written by Judge Advocate David Collins, who was also Governor Phillip’s Secretary and close friend and adviser, this was the last of the First Fleet journals and the most detailed and painstaking of all descriptions of the voyage and first settlement. The second volume, based almost entirely on the papers of Governor Hunter supplemented by official records and dispatches, is significantly more uncommon than the first volume. It is of great importance, both for its chronicle of later events and for the narratives of voyages and expeditions of discovery undertaken in the intervening years. These include the first printing of Flinders’s log of his northern voyage of 1799 in the Norfolk along the Queensland coast, as well as the inland expeditions of John Price and Henry Hacking that include the first report of the existence of the koala, the earliest recorded sighting of a wombat on mainland Australia and the first report of the discovery of the lyre-bird, which is here described and illustrated in colour for the first time. In particular, this second volume is of high Victorian interest. Through his friend and collaborator, Governor John Hunter, Collins had access to the journal of George Bass. This he reproduces in detail, a fact that is noted on the titlepage of the second volume stating that it included “an account of a voyage performed by Captain Flinders and Mr Bass; by which the existence of a Strait separating Van Diemen’s Land from the continent of New Holland was ascertained. Abstracted from the Journal of Mr. Bass”. This was the only publication of Bass’s journal of the discovery of the strait that bears his name. Ferguson, 263 and 350; Hill 2, 335 (first volume only); Wantrup, 19 and 20. Estimate $20,000/30,000 Illustrated opposite

title: DARLING, Henry C. STATEMENT IN REFUTATION of Accusations made by Mr.
description: DARLING, Henry C. STATEMENT IN REFUTATION of Accusations made by Mr. Hume, M.P., and others, against Lieut.-Gen. Darling, Governor of New South Wales. By Henry C. Darling, Major General. These three rare papers comprise a comprehensive record of legislation enacted by Governor Darling in New South Wales, including his repressive censorship laws. These laws and ordinances, gathered together here, were published periodically for the information of Members of Parliament. Ferguson, 1188, recording the National Library copy only and noting that the last page consists of an endorsement only; this copy is apparently a variant, with an “Index” to Darling’s 1826 Acts and Ordinances on the penultimate and final pages; Ferguson, 1433 and 1550. title: DUMONT D’URVILLE, Jules Sébastien César.
description: DUMONT D’URVILLE, Jules Sébastien César. VOYAGE DE LA CORVETTE L’ASTROLABE exécuté par Ordre du Roi, pendant les années 1826-1827-1828-1829, sous le commandement de M.J. Dumont d’Urville, Capitaine de Vaisseau. Publié Par Ordonnement de Sa Majesté. Histoire du Voyage. [together with] Atlas [Historique]; with Zoologie par MM Quoy et Gaimard, with Atlas Zoologie; with Botanique par MM. A. Lesson et A. Richard, with Atlas Botanique; and Faune Entomologique par le docteur Boisduval, with atlas Entomologique. Text: Historique in five volumes, octavo, with 8 engraved plates of aboriginal ceremonies, and numerous woodcut illustrations, in contemporary calf-backed paste paper boards; Zoologie, Botanique, and Entomologie in the original printed wrappers, some spines split, spotted foxing. Atlases: Historique in two volumes, super royal folio, with engraved titlepage, portrait frontispiece, and 247 lithographed maps and plates as called for, Zooologie with 192 engraved plates, the Mollusques with pale staining throughout, Botanique/Entomologique with 80 engraved plates: all entirely uncoloured, occasional spotting, two plates marked, loose in original cloth-backed papered boards (two spines lacking) with paper labels and ribbon ties. Paris, J. Tastu, 1830-34. First edition. The scientific voyage of the Astrolabe was arguably the most important and the most influential nineteenth-century French grand voyage to the Pacific. In addition to its comprehensive hydrographical work, especially in New Zealand, the Astrolabe scientists made extensive scientific observations and vast collections of natural history. The outstanding results of the expedition were published in thirteen text volumes and five large atlases from 1830 to 1835. These atlases contain what are generally acknowledged to be some of the finest plates ever produced of the natural history, topography, and anthropology of the Australasian and South-west Pacific (in this set all plates are uncoloured). Most of the fine topographical views are after Louis Auguste de Sainson. The official account of the voyage is rarely found complete. The present lot comprises Dumont d’Urville’s complete five-volume narrative account of the expedition, the Histoire, with its complete Atlas Historique bound in two parts; Quoy and Gaimard’s Atlas Zoologique in two parts, and Lesson and Richard’s Atlas Botanique, bound with Vauthier’s Atlas Entomologique. Bagnall, 1687 (part); Davidson, pp. 115-6 (part); Ferguson, 1341 (part); Hill 2, 504 (part); Hocken, p. 47 (part); Sabin, 21210 (part); Wantrup, 333 (part). Estimate $30,000/40,000 Lot 34

title: DUMONT D’URVILLE, Jules Sébastien.
description: DUMONT D’URVILLE, Jules Sébastien. VOYAGE PITTORESQUE AUTOUR DU MONDE: Résumé General des Voyages de Découvertes. Two volumes, quarto, folding maps, numerous plates and illustrations, pale foxing, contemporary quarter calf, rebacked with the worn original spines retained. Paris, Chez. L. Tenré, 1834-5. Estimate $200/400

title: EDEN, William (traditional misattribution).
description: EDEN, William (traditional misattribution). THE HISTORY OF NEW HOLLAND, from its First Discovery in 1616, to the Present Time. With a Particular Account of its Produce and Inhabitants; and a Description of Botany Bay: also, A List of the Naval, Marine, Military, and Civil Establishment. To which is prefixed, An Introductory Discourse on Banishment, by the Right Honourable William Eden. Octavo, with two folding maps handcoloured in outline (neat strengthening on verso of two folds), an appealing copy in tree calf of the period, sympathetically rebacked retaining the original spine label. London, Printed for John Stockdale, 1787. First edition. This important First Fleet book, one of the earliest descriptions of Australia, was written when the expedition to settle New Holland was first proposed publicly in 1786-7. The prominent Picadilly bookseller and publisher, John Stockdale, published the work aiming “to present at one view a connected description of the whole country of New Holland” to a public anxious for information on Botany Bay and the proposed thief colony there. The preface and text discuss the transportation of offenders, with an “Introductory Discourse on Banishment” by William Eden, to whom authorship of the whole book was for a long time attributed. Details of the fleet that was preparing to depart are given as well as a comprehensive account of what was known of the east coast of New Holland. The two fine handcoloured maps are highly regarded and show the entire continent as then known, with an inset map of Botany Bay, and a large folding world map with the “passage from England to Botany Bay in New Holland 1787” showing the route the First Fleet would take. Stockdale was exceptionally well-connected in official circles and this and other works that he published in 1786-7 relating to the proposed Botany Bay experiment were almost certainly prepared with official approval. These livres de circonstance, as Eris O’Brien called them, were essentially part of a publicity campaign by the pro-Botany-Bay lobby within Whitehall circles. Beddie, 27; Davidson, pp. 79–81 (“an extremely interesting work and an essential inclusion in all comprehensive collections”); Ferguson, 24; Holmes, 66. Estimate $3000/5000

title: EDEN, William. PRINCIPLES OF PENAL LAW. Octavo, a crisp copy, bound without the half-title in contemporary calf, corners
description: EDEN, William. PRINCIPLES OF PENAL LAW. Octavo, a crisp copy, bound without the half-title in contemporary calf, corners rubbed, modern rebacking to match, with the engraved bookplate of Viscount Sydney. London, B. White and T. Cadell, in the Strand, 1771. Second edition, an interesting association copy from the library of Viscount Sydney. While at Oxford in the 1760s Eden was influenced by the lectures of William Blackstone and shifted away from a career in the church to a career in law, being admitted to the Bar in 1768. In this book he argued for a philosophy of reform rather than punishment in the criminal law. He was closely involved in legislation to solve the problem of the hulks in the 1770s and so indirectly with the formulation of the Botany Bay ‘experiment’. His “Discourse on Banishment” was, consequently, a natural addition to Stockdale’s History of New Holland (see previous lot). ESTC T144607. Estimate $300/500

title: FIELD, Judge Barron. GEOGRAPHICAL MEMOIRS ON NEW SOUTH WALES; by various hands: Containing an account of the Surveyor Ge
description: FIELD, Judge Barron. GEOGRAPHICAL MEMOIRS ON NEW SOUTH WALES; by various hands: Containing an account of the Surveyor General’s late expedition to two new ports; the discovery of Moreton Bay River, with the adventures for seven months there of two shipwrecked men; a route from Bathurst to Liverpool Plains; Together with other papers on the Aborigines, the geology, the botany, the timber, the astronomy, and the meteorology of New South Wales and Van Diemen’s Land. Octavo, with aquatint frontispiece (faint marking of one corner), two botanical plates, four folding maps (one with a coupe of pale blots), entirely uncut, period-style half calf and marbled boards by Aquarius, spine with raised bands and gilt in compartments, double contrasting labels. London, John Murray, 1825. First edition, first issue. Of high exploration interest, Field’s book includes, among many other papers, an account of Allan Cunningham’s important exploration to the Liverpool Plains, Currie’s excursion to the southward of Lake George, the journal of Barron Field’s own trip across the Blue Mountains, and, perhaps most importantly, two accounts of Oxley’s 1823 Moreton Bay expedition (otherwise unpublished). The volume is illustrated by a fine frontispiece view of the Campbell River by John William Lewin, as well as folding maps and botanical plates. Ferguson, 1009; Richards, 84; Wantrup, 108. Estimate $1500/2000

title: FINN, Edmund, ‘Garryowen’. THE CHRONICLES OF EARLY MELBOURNE 1835 TO 1852. Historical, Anecdotal and Personal.
description: FINN, Edmund, ‘Garryowen’. THE CHRONICLES OF EARLY MELBOURNE 1835 TO 1852. Historical, Anecdotal and Personal. Two volumes, quarto, illustrations throughout, name cut from corner of each title page, one gathering with sealed marginal tears, original publisher’s dark crimson roan, decorated in gilt, all edges gilt, corners rubbing. Melbourne, Fergusson and Mitchell, 1888. First edition: now scarce. A highly detailed and important account of early Melbourne settlement by one of the city’s earliest residents and journalists. Ferguson, 9609. Estimate $400/600

title: FOX, Lady Mary, and others.
description: FOX, Lady Mary, and others. ACCOUNT OF AN EXPEDITION to the Interior of New Holland. Edited by Lady Mary Fox. Duodecimo, with the half-title but without the alien advertisements sometimes found, half red morocco and marbled boards of the period, spine with raised bands, gilt, marbled edges and endpapers, the F. Hobill Cole (with booklabel), F.G. Coles, and Davidson copy, with bookplates. London, Richard Bentley, 1837. First edition: a nicely associated copy with a presentation inscription on the title, “Little Holland House, June 1837. J.T. Graves Esqr. from the Honble. Caroline Fox”. A bizarre tale of an exploring expedition which set out from Bathurst in 1835 to penetrate further into the interior of New South Wales, where the explorers encounter a group of English-speaking native inhabitants. Ferguson, 2264. Estimate $400/600

title: GILES, Ernest. AUSTRALIA TWICE TRAVERSED. The romance of exploration, being a narrative compiled from the journals of fi
description: GILES, Ernest. AUSTRALIA TWICE TRAVERSED. The romance of exploration, being a narrative compiled from the journals of five exploring expeditions into and through Central Australia, and Western Australia, from 1872 to 1876. Two volumes, octavo, with maps and plates, all edges gilt, modern calf by Edward Congden, with his typescript description loosely inserted. London, Sampson Low, 1889. First edition of the collected narratives of Ernest Giles’s expeditions. “Giles’s claim to be the last Australian explorer is perhaps a little exaggerated, but he was undeniably the last great explorer. The very scarce two-volume account of his life’s work in the vast unknown tracts of the Australian continent is fundamental to a collection of Australian exploration books...” (Wantrup). Ferguson, 9914; Wantrup 202a. Estimate $1500/2000

title: GOVETT, William Romaine.
description: GOVETT, William Romaine. SKETCHES OF NEW SOUTH WALES. No. I [– No. XX]. Twenty parts in one volume, small folio, with woodcut illustrations throughout, a fine set in modern half blue morocco, the Davidson copy with bookplate. London, Saturday Magazine, May 1836 – September 1837. Scarce: the complete series of twenty parts. This was the only contemporary printing of this interesting and valuable account of New South Wales, written by William Romaine Govett, one of Major Thomas Livingstone Mitchell’s assistant-surveyors. Govett was engaged between 1829 and 1833 in the extensive survey of the colony that Governor Darling had directed Mitchell to complete. Govett’s account deals with the country he had helped to survey, the habits of the Aborigines, who interested him greatly, life in Sydney, the natural productions of Eastern Australia, and so on. In the course of his work on the Government Survey he discovered Govett’s Leap in the Blue Mountains, named by Mitchell in his honour. Each of the parts is illustrated by woodcuts of Australian scenery, the Aborigines, etc., most half-page folio in size. These fine illustrations are all after Govett’s drawings, with the exception of one after Charles Rodius. Ferguson, 2175 (noting only the first 14 parts in error); Kerr, pp. 315-6. See also ADB, 1:467-8. Estimate $1000/1500

title: GREAT BRITAIN: PARLIAMENT. WESTERN AND SOUTHERN AUSTRALIA. RETURN TO AN ADDRESS… for No.
description: GREAT BRITAIN: PARLIAMENT. WESTERN AND SOUTHERN AUSTRALIA. RETURN TO AN ADDRESS… for No. 1. Return of all the expenses defrayed in the Country in the Colony of Western Australia… Copy of a Despatch from Governor Sir James Stirling… Returns for South Australia, similar… Foolscap folio, sewn as issued, with two other pieces in a bookform box. [London], Ordered by the House of Commons, to be Printed, 6 August 1838. Ferguson, 2511. + SOUTH AUSTRALIA. RETURN TO AN ADDRESS… for Returns of the Quantity of Land in South Australia sold… Foolscap folio, sewn as issued. [London], Ordered by the House of Commons, to be Printed, 10 April 1840. Both pieces with the pencilled ownership signature of C.A.S. Hawker. Ferguson, 3002. + A duplicate copy of the 1840 report. Estimate $150/300

title: GREGORY, A.C. NORTH AUSTRALIAN EXPLORING EXPEDITION: Copy Correspondence [and] Copy of Additional Correspondence.
description: GREGORY, A.C. NORTH AUSTRALIAN EXPLORING EXPEDITION: Copy Correspondence [and] Copy of Additional Correspondence. Two pieces, foolscap folio, the first piece sewn as issued, the second disbound and with stamped pagination, trimmed and with chipped left margin. Melbourne, John Ferres, 1855. Scarce: preparatory to Gregory’s great North Australian Expedition; includes letters from Charles Sturt and John Lort Stokes. The second paper not noted by McLaren. Estimate $300/500

title: HARRIS, Alexander. SETTLERS AND CONVICTS; or, Recollections of Sixteen Years’ Labour in the Australian Backwoods.
description: HARRIS, Alexander. SETTLERS AND CONVICTS; or, Recollections of Sixteen Years’ Labour in the Australian Backwoods. By an Emigrant Mechanic. Duodecimo, original publisher’s cloth, spine ends fraying, the spine lettered and decorated in gilt, all edges gilt, the Davidson copy with bookplate. London, G. Cox, 1852. Exiled by his family to New South Wales in 1825, Alexander Harris worked as a cedar getter until leaving Australia in 1841. Returning to London he became associated with the movement to promote emigration and wrote or co-wrote several works, most notably this classic account of Australian backwoods life. Essentially a fictionalised presentation of his own experiences, this is acknowledged as the most significant early articulation of the spirit of Australian egalitarianism. This is the so-called ‘second edition’ (in fact a re-dated re-impression). It was printed from the stereotyped plates of the 1847 first edition, which was itself more than once reprinted with title-page dated 1847 (including re-issues in two parts in Knight’s monthly volume series) before this re-dated 1852 impression. Ferguson, 10254. Provenance: F. Hobill Cole with booklabel. Estimate $100/200

title: HUME, Hamilton. A BRIEF STATEMENT OF FACTS in connection with an Overland Expedition from Lake George to Port Phillip, i
description: HUME, Hamilton. A BRIEF STATEMENT OF FACTS in connection with an Overland Expedition from Lake George to Port Phillip, in 1824. Octavo, with lithographed portrait frontispiece (pale damp mark), original limp cloth, printed label on the front board, H.L. White copy with Belltrees bookplate. Yass, J.J. Brown, 1874. description: INTERNATIONAL EXHIBITION. SYDNEY, 1879. NOTES ON THE SYDNEY INTERNATIONAL EXHIBITION OF 1879. With Photo-Type Illustrations. title: LOCKE, John. REMARKABLE DISCOVERIES IN CENTRAL AUSTRALIA, WITH AN ILLUSTRATIVE MAP: A Paper read before the Royal Dublin
description: LOCKE, John. REMARKABLE DISCOVERIES IN CENTRAL AUSTRALIA, WITH AN ILLUSTRATIVE MAP: A Paper read before the Royal Dublin Society, March 18, 1861. Octavo, pp. 16 + double-page map (this with damp stain), bound with the original green wrappers in old binder’s cloth, the H.L. White / Rodney Davidson copy with bookplates. Dublin, Printed at the University Press, by M.H. Gill, 1861. Locke was a regular contributor to the Royal Dublin Society, reading and publishing many papers on geographical and related subjects in the 1860s. His annotations indicate that he was exceptionally well connected to officials and other interested parties throughout the Australian colonies and his papers are uncommonly well-informed making them much more substantial than mere journalism. This is a presentation copy of his first paper on Australian exploration and reports the results of Stuart’s great fourth expedition that had been cut short at Attack Creek. Ferguson, 11693. Estimate $4000/6000

title: LOCKE, John. REMARKABLE DISCOVERIES IN CENTRAL AUSTRALIA, with an improved map, showing the additional routes of Stuart
description: LOCKE, John. REMARKABLE DISCOVERIES IN CENTRAL AUSTRALIA, with an improved map, showing the additional routes of Stuart and Burke: Second Paper read before the Royal Dublin Society, December 24, 1861. Octavo, pp. 14 + double-page map, original russet wrappers, extremities slightly worn, housed in modern card wrappers in papered slipcase, the Davidson copy with bookplate. Dublin, Printed at the University Press, by M.H. Gill, 1862. In this second pamphlet Locke continues his detailed and well-informed discussion of recent Australian exploration, concentrating on Stuart’s fifth expedition and the disastrous Victorian Exploring Expedition under Burke and Wills. Presentation copy to the London Institution, inscribed by the author on the front wrapper, dated from Dublin, 23 August, 1861. Ferguson, 11694. Estimate $4000/6000

title: MACARTHUR, James. NEW SOUTH WALES; ITS PRESENT STATE AND FUTURE PROSPECTS: being a Statement, with Documentary Evidence,
description: MACARTHUR, James. NEW SOUTH WALES; ITS PRESENT STATE AND FUTURE PROSPECTS: being a Statement, with Documentary Evidence, submitted in support of Petitions to His Majesty and Parliament. Octavo, with handcoloured folding map (pale foxing), with half-title, original green moiré cloth, split at the bottom of the front joint but sound, the Davidson copy with bookplate. London, D. Walther, 1837. First edition: an excellent presentation copy of this important political statement prepared by James Macarthur and edited anonymously for him by noted British librarian Edward Edwards, is a comprehensive and well-documented account of the colony from the social, political and economic point of view. The present copy was presented by William Macarthur, brother and partner of James, and is inscribed on the free front endpaper to “Mr. [Peter?] Gardner from Wm Macarthur, Esq of Camden”, and with Gardner’s bookplate. Ferguson, 2304. Estimate $800/1000

title: MACARTHUR, Major Edward.
description: MACARTHUR, Major Edward. COLONIAL POLICY OF 1840 AND 1841, as illustrated by the Governor’s despatches, and proceedings of the Legislative Council of New South Wales. Octavo, with a handcoloured map, the title soiled, a defect in the bottom fore-margins of the first and second leaves made good, one opening with margin marked, entirely uncut and largely unopened, in more recent quarter calf. London, John Murray, 1841. Rare: advocating emigration and discussing at length the British government’s land policy in New South Wales. A distinguished soldier, Sir Edward Macarthur was the eldest son of John Macarthur, the great perturbator. As a very young man he was involved in his father’s deposition of Governor Bligh but, unlike his father, he went on to serve his country with distinction. Until 1851 he was stationed in London, actively representing Australian interests there. This is one – and the more important – of two pamphlets he published in the 1840s promoting the cause of emigration to the Australian colonies. He was later the highly respected peace-making Governor of Victoria after the Eureka Rebellion, which was the culmination of his predecessor, Hotham’s, disastrous administration. Ferguson, 3241. Estimate $300/500 Lot 49

title: MITCHELL, Thomas Livingstone.
description: MITCHELL, Thomas Livingstone. THREE EXPEDITIONS INTO THE INTERIOR OF EASTERN AUSTRALIA, with descriptions of the recently explored region of Australia Felix, and of the present Colony of New South Wales. Two volumes, octavo, with plates (some coloured), and coloured maps, pale offsetting of plates and maps, large folding map with neatly repaired short tears, original embossed cloth, gilt, both spines with minor restoration, a fine set, Novar of Raith copy with Emery Walker engraved bookplate in each volume. London, T. & W. Boone, 1838. First edition: three expeditions of the greatest importance, both for the discoveries made and for the precision with which Mitchell was capable of surveying. The first expedition (1831-2) surveyed the area between the Castlereagh and the Gwydir Rivers; the second (1835) set out to trace and chart sections of the Murray and Darling rivers; the third and most important (1836) was intended to complete the survey of the Darling but culminated in the discovery of Australia Felix in 1836. Billot, 129; Ferguson, 2553; Wantrup, 124a. Estimate $1000/2000

title: MITCHELL, Thomas Livingstone.
description: MITCHELL, Thomas Livingstone. SUPPLEMENT TO THE NEW SOUTH WALES GOVERNMENT GAZETTE… Thursday, December 31, 1846... Camp by Snodgrass Lagoon, 14th December, 1846 [drop title]. Foolscap folio, pp. [6] (numbered 1640 – 1643, last blank), printed in double column on white paper. Sydney, W.W. Davies, Government Printer, 1846. Rare: printing, in the Government Gazette, of one of Mitchell’s reports of his expedition to tropical Australia in 1845-6 in search of the north-west flowing river and an overland route to Port Essington. This was Mitchell’s fourth and last expedition. Wantrup, p. 203. Estimate $400/600

title: MUDIE, James. THE FELONRY OF NEW SOUTH WALES: Being a faithful picture of the real romance of life in Botany Bay.
description: MUDIE, James. THE FELONRY OF NEW SOUTH WALES: Being a faithful picture of the real romance of life in Botany Bay. With Anecdotes of Botany Bay Society. Octavo, the folding map of Sydney with a stamp in the margin, faint stamp on title, recent half calf, top edge gilt, others uncut, the Davidson copy with bookplate. London, For the Author, 1837. First edition of this famous and controversial book, a vitriolic account of New South Wales attacking the liberal administration of Governor Bourke. Mudie insulted and libelled many leading members of colonial society, and in 1840, when he foolishly returned to Sydney, he was publicly horsewhipped by the son of Judge Kinsella, who had been libelled in the book. When Mudie was subsequently awarded £50 damages the sum was raised by public subscription on the spot. The Blaxland family had notes and corrections printed on three octavo leaves that were to be cut into narrow slips and pasted on the margins of Mudie’s book. The notes appear to have been pasted into very few copies and have always been considered very rare. Loosely inserted in this copy is the limited edition of James R. Tyrrell’s Marginal Notes to Mudie’s Felonry of New South Wales from Vincent Dowling’s and other copies, published in Sydney in 1922 in an edition said to comprise only 25 copies. Ferguson, 2312. Provenance: Travers Borrow, with ownership inscription. Estimate $300/500

title: NAPIER, Francis. NOTES OF A VOYAGE from New South Wales to the North Coast of Australia, from the Journal of the late Francis Napier.
description: NAPIER, Francis. NOTES OF A VOYAGE from New South Wales to the North Coast of Australia, from the Journal of the late Francis Napier. Octavo, with mounted photographic portrait, eight lithographed plates, four folding maps, one full-page map (p. 70), and a few other illustrations in the text, original blue cloth (bit marked), gilt. [Glasgow, Privately Printed, 1876]. Inscribed presentation copy from the editor (as often). Extremely scarce: the posthumous first edition of Francis Napier’s journal of Cadell’s 1867-9 Northern Territory Expedition, the only separately-published account. Ferguson, 13058; Wantrup, 102. Estimate $300/500

title: NORTHERN TERRITORY. NORTHERN TERRITORY CORRESPONDENCE [bound with] PROCEEDINGS OF SURVEYING SCHOONER “BEATRICE”. Foolsca
description: NORTHERN TERRITORY. NORTHERN TERRITORY CORRESPONDENCE [bound with] PROCEEDINGS OF SURVEYING SCHOONER “BEATRICE”. Foolscap folio, two pieces bound in one volume, neat modern binder’s linen with leather label. Adelaide, Ordered by the House of Assembly to be printed, 28th September 1866. Northern Territory ‘First Fleet’: the voyage of H.M. Surveying Schooner Beatrice was a key undertaking associated with the first attempt to establish a permanent settlement in South Australia’s recently annexed Northern Territory. South Australian Parliamentary Papers Numbers 79 and 80 of 1866. Estimate $100/200

title: OXLEY, John. JOURNALS OF TWO EXPEDITIONS INTO THE INTERIOR OF NEW SOUTH WALES, undertaken by order of the British Govern
description: OXLEY, John. JOURNALS OF TWO EXPEDITIONS INTO THE INTERIOR OF NEW SOUTH WALES, undertaken by order of the British Government in the Years 1817-18. By John Oxley, Surveyor General of the Territory and Lieutenant of the Royal Navy. With Maps and Views of the Interior, or newly discovered country. Quarto, with the sectional title, one folding engraved plate, five aquatint plates (two handcoloured), three folding charts, and two folding tables; a fine copy beautifully bound in period style by Aquarius in half tan calf and marbled boards, marbled edges and endpapers, the spine elaborately decorated in gilt, with contrasting label and inlays of red morocco. London, John Murray, 1820. First edition of the foundation work of Australian inland exploration and the first detailed description of the interior of New South Wales to be published. Surveyor-General John Oxley’s narrative of his two major expeditions, issued in an edition of only 500 copies, includes a fine hand-coloured aquatint portrait of an Aboriginal chief by John William Lewin, as well as an evocative series of aquatint landscape views drawn by Major James Taylor from sketches by George William Evans. Ferguson, 796; Wantrup, 107. Estimate $5000/7000

title: O’HARA, James. THE HISTORY OF NEW SOUTH WALES. Second Edition.
description: O’HARA, James. THE HISTORY OF NEW SOUTH WALES. Second Edition. Octavo, bound without the half-title in speckled calf of the period, sympathetically rebacked at some time with new endpapers, contrasting spine label, the Davidson copy with bookplate. London, Printed for J. Hatchard, 1818. This was the first general history of New South Wales and Van Diemen’s Land that was not merely a compilation, or plagiarism, of earlier first-hand accounts. O’Hara’s book is of particular note for its record of the otherwise virtually unobtainable reports of the explorations of George William Evans, whose discoveries proved to be of greater consequence than those of his predecessors and contemporaries. First published anonymously the year before by O’Hara himself, this is the second Hatchard issue of the original sheets, the third issue overall. All early issues are very scarce. “The first true history of the colony... O’Hara provides the best picture of the first half of Macquarie’s rule, the Golden Age, that we have between two covers” (Wantrup). Ferguson, 725; Wantrup, 40 (note) and p. 110. Estimate $800/1200

title: PERON, François, and Louuis Claude de Saulces de FREYCINET. VOYAGE DE DECOUVERTES AUX TERRES AUSTRALES, Sur les corvette
description: PERON, François, and Louuis Claude de Saulces de FREYCINET. VOYAGE DE DECOUVERTES AUX TERRES AUSTRALES, Sur les corvettes le Geographe, le Naturaliste, et la goelette le Casuarina, pendant les annees 1800, 1801, 1802, 1803 et 1804… Two volumes, quarto, frontispiece portrait and two folding tables, early inked number on titles, occasional pale foxing, original morocco-backed paste paper boards, spines eroded at foot, corners worn. Paris, l’Imprimerie Royale, 1807 – 1816. First edition of the Historique text (only), the official account of the important Baudin voyage to Australia and the Pacific, the second volume completed by Freycinet after Peron’s death. Estimate $600/1000

title: PHILLIP, Governor Arthur.
description: PHILLIP, Governor Arthur. THE VOYAGE OF GOVERNOR PHILLIP TO BOTANY BAY; with an Account of the Establishment of the Colonies of Port Jackson and Norfolk Island... to which are added the Journals of Lieuts. Shortland, Watts, Ball and Capt. Marshall. Quarto, with 54 engraved plates and charts, pale offsetting, Sydney Cove map splitting at fold, bound in contemporary calf, sympathetically rebacked, retaining the original endpapers, all edges yellow. London, John Stockdale, 1789. First edition of the foundation book for New South Wales, the ‘official’ – or at least government-endorsed – account of the First Fleet voyage and settlement at Sydney Cove. In this copy the plate at page 150 is in the rare “Wulpine” state; the engraved title is in the second state. Ayer/Zimmer, 491; Davidson, pp. 70-2; Ferguson, 47; Hill 2, 1347; Wantrup, 5a. Estimate $3000/5000

title: PHILLIP, Governor Arthur.
description: PHILLIP, Governor Arthur. THE VOYAGE OF GOVERNOR PHILLIP TO BOTANY BAY; with an Account of the Establishment of the Colonies of Port Jackson and Norfolk Island... third Edition. Octavo, with engraved frontispiece and title, pale mark at foot and margin, engraved plates and charts (most folding) offset to facing leaves, tear repaired in Sketch of Sydney Cove, early inked signature on title, with a folding table at p. 238, modern mottled calf with earlier title label retained, the spine sunned. London, John Stockdale, 1790. The third edition, reset and printed as an octavo. Ferguson, 91. Estimate $1000/1500

title: STUART, John McDouall.
description: STUART, John McDouall. MR. STUART’S EXPLORATION IN SOUTH AUSTRALIA. Foolscap folio, with a large folding map, disbound. Melbourne, John Ferres, Government Printer, 1858. The very scarce publication by the Victorian parliament of the official journal of John McDouall Stuart’s first expedition. McLaren, 15457. Estimate $400/600

title: STUART, John McDouall.
description: STUART, John McDouall. JOHN McDOUALL STUART’S EXPLORATIONS across the Continent of Australia with charts 1861-62. Octavo, frontispiece large folding map, occasional spotting, a good copy in original lightly worn cloth-backed card wrappers. Melbourne, F.F. Baillière, 1863. First edition. Ferguson, 16380; Wantrup, 161. Estimate $300/500

title: TENCH, Watkin. A COMPLETE ACCOUNT OF THE SETTLEMENT AT PORT JACKSON IN NEW SOUTH WALES, including an accurate descriptio
description: TENCH, Watkin. A COMPLETE ACCOUNT OF THE SETTLEMENT AT PORT JACKSON IN NEW SOUTH WALES, including an accurate description of the situation of the colony; of the natives; and of its natural productions. Quarto, with an engraved folding map, the final leaf with slight paper weakness and invisible paper tape at head, a touch of largely pale spotting but an excellent copy, top edge gilt, others uncut, in a signed binding by Gordon Hughes of dark brown morocco, the boards with marginal fillets, gilt dots on the board edges, panelled spine with prominently raised bands, the bands produced on to the surface of the boards with stylised gilt ornaments in imitation of medieval ties, wide inner leather dentelles with contrasting inlays at the corners. London, G. Nicol and J. Sewell, 1793. First edition of Captain Watkin Tench’s second book on New South Wales. Tench was the only First Fleet chronicler to publish more than one book. He had returned to England with other marines in the Gorgon in 1792 and this second, grander, account of the colony was published over a year later, at the end of 1793. Tench “completes his account of the first years of the colony and brings his record of events down to the end of the first four years of settlement. The map and text give important and full details of the early expeditions of discovery to the south and to the west, including those which Tench led himself. As an accurate, well-written and acutely observed account of the earliest years of Australia’s colonisation, it is a most important addition to any collection of Australian books. description: WHITE, John. JOURNAL OF A VOYAGE TO NEW SOUTH WALES with Sixty-five Plates of Nondescript Animals, Birds, Lizards, Serpents, curious Cones of Trees and other Natural Productions. Quarto, with engraved titlepage, 65 handcoloured plates on Whatman paper, bound with the rare 4-page terminal advertisements that were not issued with all copies, a fine copy bound in contemporary polished tree calf, the spine with raised bands and elaborately gilt in compartments with ship ornaments and the silhouette of a navigator (Captain James Cook?) heralded by a trumpeting angel, contrasting spine label, all edges yellow, some discreet expert repairs to the joints and extremities, with the engraved Luton Library bookplate of the Marquis of Bute, an exceptional binding. London, J. Debrett, 1790. A superb copy – one of the most handsome copies we have seen – of the much-prized superior de luxe handcoloured issue of this celebrated First Fleet journal with the fine natural history plates on Whatman paper and in original publisher’s handcolouring. In this special handcoloured form, it is the earliest and one of the best and most appealing of Australian colour-illustrated natural history books. John White was the chief surgeon on the First Fleet and Surgeon-general to the settlement, whose most remarkable, if still little recognised, achievement was the minuscule mortality rates among the convicts on the long voyage from England to New South Wales, in what is still one of the largest mass movements of humanity ever undertaken. He commenced his journal with the sailing of the First Fleet and continued his often personal chronicle through the first ten months of settlement at Sydney Cove, including “many circumstances omitted by Governor Arthur Phillip and others” (Hill). A characteristic scientific gentleman of the age, his interest in Australian natural history was the inspiration for the publication of this journal, with its fine plates of Australian birds, reptiles, fish, plants, and animals. It is particularly noteworthy among the First Fleet journals for its scientific descriptions and engravings of many hitherto undescribed species. Publication of this account was arranged by Thomas Wilson, a Fellow of the Linnaean Society, who engaged Dr. George Shaw to provide scientific descriptions of the birds, reptiles and fish, Dr. James Smith to describe the plants, and the celebrated anatomist Dr. John Hunter to describe the animals. The plates were prepared by leading natural history artists, most notably Sarah Stone and Frederick Nodder, from live and stuffed specimens sent by White as well as from drawings and sketches prepared for him in the colony.
